claim: Attention profoundly influences information processing in the brain.
source: Attention profoundly influences information processing in the brain (Posner and Petersen, 1990; Treisman and Gelade, 1980; Rayner, 1998)
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on attention mechanisms.

claim: Attention is traditionally viewed as a mechanism to allocate limited central processing resources.
source: At the computational level, attention is traditionally viewed as a mechanism to allocate limited central processing resources (Kahneman, 1973; Franconeri et al., 2013; Lennie, 2003; Carrasco, 2011; Borji and Itti, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical frameworks on attention.

claim: Recent studies propose that attention is a mechanism to optimize task performance, even in conditions where the processing resource is not clearly constrained.
source: More recent studies, however, propose that attention is a mechanism to optimize task performance, even in conditions where the processing resource is not clearly constrained (Dayan et al., 2000; Gottlieb et al., 2014; Legge et al., 2002; Liu and Reichle, 2010; Najemnik and Geisler, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent theoretical work on attention optimization.

claim: The optimization hypothesis can explain the attention distribution in a range of well-controlled learning and decision-making tasks.
source: The optimization hypothesis can explain the attention distribution in a range of well-controlled learning and decision-making tasks (Najemnik and Geisler, 2005; Navalpakkam et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies demonstrating optimization in attention.

claim: The optimization hypothesis is rarely tested in complex processing tasks for which the optimal strategy is not obvious.
source: but is rarely tested in complex processing tasks for which the optimal strategy is not obvious.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, inferred from the literature review.

claim: Reading is one of the most common and most sophisticated human behaviors.
source: Reading is one of the most common and most sophisticated human behaviors (Li et al., 2022; Gagl et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on reading behavior.

claim: Reading is strongly regulated by attention.
source: and it is strongly regulated by attention: Since readers can only recognize a couple of words within one fixation, they have to overtly shift their fixation to read a line of text (Rayner, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to established reading research and knowledge about visual processing limitations.

claim: Eye movements serve as an overt expression of attention allocation during reading.
source: Thus, eye movements serve as an overt expression of attention allocation during reading (Rayner, 1998; Clifton et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to reading research literature.

claim: Computational modeling of eye movements has mostly focused on normal reading of single sentences.
source: Computational modeling of the eye movements has mostly focused on normal reading of single sentences.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature, inferred from the review.

claim: It has been proposed that eye movements are programmed to minimize the number of eye movements.
source: At the computational level, it has been proposed that the eye movements are programmed to, for example, minimize the number of eye movements (Legge et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work on eye movement optimization.

claim: Models such as the E-Z reader can accurately predict the eye movement trajectory with high temporal and spatial resolution.
source: At the algorithmic and implementational level, models such as the E-Z reader (Reichle et al., 2003) can accurately predict the eye movement trajectory with high temporal and spatial resolution.
evidence: Supported by citation to the E-Z reader model literature.

claim: Everyday reading behavior often engages reading of a multiline passage and generally has a clear goal.
source: Everyday reading behavior, however, often engages reading of a multiline passage and generally has a clear goal, for example, information retrieval or inference generation (White et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation and general knowledge about reading behavior.

claim: Few models have considered how the reading goal modulates reading behaviors.
source: Few models, however, have considered how the reading goal modulates reading behaviors.
evidence: This is a characterization of the literature gap, inferred from the review.

claim: DNN models equipped with attention mechanisms have approached and even surpassed mean human performance on goal-directed reading tasks.
source: Recent advances in DNN models, however, provide a potential tool to solve this computational problem since DNN models equipped with attention mechanisms have approached and even surpassed mean human performance on goal-directed reading tasks (Lan et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to DNN model performance literature.

claim: Task-optimized DNNs can explain the neural response properties in a range of visual and language processing tasks.
source: Furthermore, recent studies have provided strong evidence that task-optimized DNN can indeed explain the neural response properties in a range of visual and language processing tasks (Yamins et al., 2014; Kell et al., 2018; Goldstein et al., 2022; Schrimpf et al., 2021; Hasson et al., 2020; Donhauser and Baillet, 2020; Rabovsky et al., 2018; Heilbron et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to neuroscience and computational modeling literature.

claim: Participants in Experiment 1 correctly answered 77.94% questions on average.
source: The participants correctly answered 77.94% questions on average and the accuracy was comparable across the six types of questions (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and Figure 1B.

claim: The orthographic model achieved 25.6% accuracy.
source: This orthographic model achieved 25.6% accuracy (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by computational model results presented in the manuscript and Figure 1B.

claim: The semantic model achieved 27.3% accuracy.
source: Another simple heuristic model only considered word-level semantic matching between the passage and option, and achieved 27.3% accuracy (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by computational model results presented in the manuscript and Figure 1B.

claim: The low accuracy of the orthographic and semantic models indicated that the reading comprehension questions could not be answered by word-level orthographic or semantic matching.
source: The low accuracy of the two models indicated that the reading comprehension questions could not be answered by word-level orthographic or semantic matching.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the low model performance data.

claim: The SAR achieved 47.6% accuracy.
source: The SAR used the bidirectional recurrent neural network (RNN) to integrate contextual information (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and achieved 47.6% accuracy.
evidence: Supported by computational model results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model performance on the reading task was 37.08 and 73%, respectively, after pre-training and fine-tuning.
source: The model performance on the reading task was 37.08 and 73%, respectively, after pre-training and fine-tuning (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by computational model results presented in the manuscript and Figure 1B.

claim: Participants spent, on average, 0.7 ± 0.2 min reading each passage.
source: The results showed that the participants spent, on average, 0.7 ± 0.2 min reading each passage (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and Figure 1C.

claim: The reading speed was 457 ± 142 words/min when divided by the number of words per passage.
source: corresponding to a reading speed of 457 ± 142 words/min when divided by the number of words per passage.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data on reading time and passage length.

claim: The reading speed was almost twice the normal reading speed for native readers.
source: The speed was almost twice the normal reading speed for native readers (Rayner, 1998), indicating a specialized reading strategy for the task.
evidence: Comparison to established reading speed norms from cited literature.

claim: The predictions of the heuristic models were not highly correlated with the human word reading time, and the predictive power was around 0.2.
source: The predictions of the heuristic models were not highly correlated with the human word reading time, and the predictive power, that is, the Pearson correlation coefficient between the predicted and real word reading time, was around 0.2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis results presented in the manuscript and supplementary figure.

claim: When the attention weights of the SAR were used to predict the human word reading time, the predictive power was about 0.1.
source: When the attention weights of the SAR were used to predict the human word reading time, the predictive power was about 0.1 (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis results presented in the manuscript and Figure 3A.

claim: The attention weights of randomly initialized transformer-based models could predict the human word reading time and the predictive power was around 0.3.
source: The attention weights of randomly initialized transformer-based models could predict the human word reading time and the predictive power, which was around 0.3, was significantly higher than the chance level and the SAR (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis results and statistical testing presented in the manuscript.

claim: The attention weights of pre-trained transformer-based models could predict the human word reading time, and the predictive power was around 0.5.
source: The attention weights of pre-trained transformer-based models could also predict the human word reading time, the predictive power was around 0.5, significantly higher than the predictive power of heuristic models, the SAR, and randomly initialized transformer-based models (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis results and statistical testing presented in the manuscript.

claim: The predictive power was further boosted for local but not global questions when the models were fine-tuned to perform the goal-directed reading task.
source: The predictive power was further boosted for local but not global questions when the models were fine-tuned to perform the goal-directed reading task (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis results comparing pre-trained and fine-tuned models.

claim: Layout features could significantly predict the word reading time.
source: Linear regression analyses revealed layout features could significantly predict the word reading time (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by regression analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The predictive power of layout features was higher for global than local questions.
source: Furthermore, the predictive power was higher for global than local questions (p=4 × 10–5, bootstrap, false discovery rate [FDR] corrected for comparisons across three features, i.e., layout features, word features, and question relevance)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of regression results between question types.

claim: Word features could significantly predict human reading time, even when the influence of layout features was regressed out.
source: Word features could also significantly predict human reading time, even when the influence of layout features was regressed out.
evidence: Supported by regression analysis controlling for layout features.

claim: A linear mixed effect model revealed significant fixed effects for question type and all text/task-related features, as well as significant interactions between question type and these text/task-related features.
source: Additionally, a linear mixed effect model revealed significant fixed effects for question type and all text/task-related features, as well as significant interactions between question type and these text/task-related features (Supplementary file 1c; Pinheiro and Bates, 2006; Kuznetsova et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by linear mixed effects model analysis results.

claim: The predictive power of the layout and word features was lower than the predictive power of attention weights of transformer-based models.
source: The predictive power of the layout and word features, however, was lower than the predictive power of attention weights of transformer-based models (p=4 × 10–5, bootstrap, FDR corrected for comparisons across two features, i.e., layout and word features).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of predictive power across different models.

claim: When the layout and word features were regressed out, the residual word reading time was still significantly predicted by the attention weights in transformer-based models.
source: When the layout and word features were regressed out, the residual word reading time was still significantly predicted by the attention weights in transformer-based models (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, predictive power about 0.3).
evidence: Supported by regression analysis controlling for text features.

claim: The annotated question relevance could significantly predict word reading time, even when the influences of layout and word features were regressed out.
source: The annotated question relevance could significantly predict word reading time, even when the influences of layout and word features were regressed out (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by regression analysis controlling for text features.

claim: When the question relevance was also regressed out, the residual word reading time was still significantly predicted by the attention weights in transformer-based models.
source: When the question relevance was also regressed out, the residual word reading time was still significantly predicted by the attention weights in transformer-based models (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, p=0.003, bootstrap, FDR corrected for comparisons across 12 models × 6 question types), but the predictive power dropped to about 0.2.
evidence: Supported by regression analysis controlling for both text features and question relevance.

claim: More than 85% of the DNN attention heads contribute to the prediction of human reading time when considering text features and question relevance as covariates.
source: Furthermore, a linear mixed effect model also revealed that more than 85% of the DNN attention heads contribute to the prediction of human reading time when considering text features and question relevance as covariates (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Supported by linear mixed effects model analysis results.

claim: For local questions, the question-relevant words were roughly uniformly distributed in the passage.
source: First, for local questions, the question-relevant words were roughly uniformly distributed in the passage, while for global questions, the question-relevant words tended to be near the passage beginning (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of question relevance annotations presented in supplementary figure.

claim: For global questions, the question-relevant words tended to be near the passage beginning.
source: First, for local questions, the question-relevant words were roughly uniformly distributed in the passage, while for global questions, the question-relevant words tended to be near the passage beginning (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of question relevance annotations presented in supplementary figure.

claim: Readers spent more time reading the passage beginning for global than local questions.
source: The eye-tracking data showed that readers also spent more time reading the passage beginning for global than local questions (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by eye-tracking data analysis presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Few lines in the passage were question relevant.
source: Second, few lines in the passage were question relevant (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: Supported by analysis of question relevance annotations presented in supplementary figure.

claim: Readers spent more time reading the line with the highest question relevance.
source: and the eye-tracking data showed that readers spent more time reading the line with the highest question relevance (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by eye-tracking data analysis presented in Figure 3D.

claim: The influence of layout features increased from early to late reading stages for global but not local questions.
source: Results showed the influence of layout features increased from early to late reading stages for global but not local questions (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by analysis of different eye-tracking measures presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The influence of word features did not strongly change between reading stages.
source: The influence of word features did not strongly change between reading stages
evidence: Supported by analysis of different eye-tracking measures.

claim: The influence of question relevance significantly increased from early to late reading stages.
source: while the influence of question relevance significantly increased from early to late reading stages (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of different eye-tracking measures presented in figures.

claim: Attention to basic text features developed early, while the influence of task mainly influenced late reading processes.
source: These results suggested that attention to basic text features developed early, while the influence of task mainly influenced late reading processes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects across reading stages.

claim: The attention weights in shallow layers were sensitive to word features in randomized, pre-trained, and fine-tuned models.
source: The attention weights in shallow layers were sensitive to word features in randomized, pre-trained, and fine-tuned models (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by layer-wise analysis of DNN attention weights presented in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Only in the fine-tuned models, the attention weights in deep layers were sensitive to question relevance.
source: Only in the fine-tuned models, however, the attention weights in deep layers were sensitive to question relevance (see Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3 for results of individual models).
evidence: Supported by layer-wise analysis of DNN attention weights presented in supplementary figures.

claim: The shallow and deep layers separately evolved text-based and goal-directed attention.
source: Therefore, the shallow and deep layers separately evolved text-based and goal-directed attention, and goal-directed attention was induced by fine-tuning on the task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the layer-wise analysis of attention weights.

claim: In Experiment 2, the reading speed was on average 298 ± 123 words/min.
source: In Experiment 2, the reading speed was on average 298 ± 123 words/min, lower than the speed in Experiment 1 (p=6 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for the comparisons across four experiments)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The reading speed in Experiment 2 was lower than the speed in Experiment 1.
source: In Experiment 2, the reading speed was on average 298 ± 123 words/min, lower than the speed in Experiment 1 (p=6 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for the comparisons across four experiments)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of reading speeds between experiments.

claim: The word reading time in Experiment 2 was better predicted by fine-tuned than pre-trained transformer-based models.
source: The word reading time was better predicted by fine-tuned than pre-trained transformer-based models (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions in Experiment 2.

claim: Compared to Experiment 1, the predictive power in Experiment 2 was higher for layout and word features, but lower for question relevance.
source: For the influence of text and task-related features, compared to Experiment 1, the predictive power in Experiment 2 was higher for layout and word features, but lower for question relevance (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Supported by comparison of regression results between experiments.

claim: For local questions in Experiment 2, the effects of question relevance significantly increased from early to late processing stages.
source: For local questions, consistent with Experiment 1, the effects of question relevance significantly increased from early to late processing stages that are separately indexed by gaze duration and counts of rereading (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by analysis of different eye-tracking measures in Experiment 2.

claim: The passage beginning effect was higher for global than local questions in Experiment 2.
source: The passage beginning effect was higher for global than local questions (Figure 5C, second column, p=2 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for the comparisons across four experiments)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of passage beginning effects in Experiment 2.

claim: The difference in passage beginning effect between global and local questions was smaller in Experiment 2 than in Experiment 1.
source: but the difference was smaller than in Experiment 1 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, p=2 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for the comparisons across four experiments).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between experiments.

claim: The question relevance effect was smaller in Experiment 2 than Experiment 1.
source: The question relevance effect was also smaller in Experiment 2 than Experiment 1 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, p=2 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for the comparisons across four experiments).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between experiments.

claim: The readers developed question type-specific strategies in Experiment 1, which led to faster reading speed and stronger task modulation of word reading time.
source: All these results indicated that the readers developed question type-specific strategies in Experiment 1, which led to faster reading speed and stronger task modulation of word reading time.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of results between Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: In Experiment 3, the reading speed was on average 506 ± 155 words/min.
source: In Experiment 3, the reading speed was on average 506 ± 155 words/min, higher than that in Experiment 2 (p=6 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for the comparisons across four experiments).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: The reading speed in Experiment 3 was higher than that in Experiment 2.
source: In Experiment 3, the reading speed was on average 506 ± 155 words/min, higher than that in Experiment 2 (p=6 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for the comparisons across four experiments).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of reading speeds between experiments.

claim: The question answering accuracy in Experiment 3 was comparable to L2 readers.
source: The question answering accuracy was comparable to L2 readers (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of accuracy data between experiments.

claim: The word reading time for native readers was slightly better predicted by fine-tuned than pre-trained transformer-based models.
source: The word reading time for native readers was slightly better predicted by fine-tuned than pre-trained transformer-based models (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions in Experiment 3.

claim: Compared to Experiment 2, the predictive power in Experiment 3 was higher for word features, but lower for layout features and question relevance.
source: For the influence of text and task-related features, compared to Experiment 2, the predictive power in Experiment 3 was higher for word features, but lower for layout features and question relevance (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Supported by comparison of regression results between experiments.

claim: For local questions in Experiment 3, the layout effect was more salient for gaze duration than for counts of rereading.
source: For local questions, the layout effect was more salient for gaze duration than for counts of rereading.
evidence: Supported by analysis of different eye-tracking measures in Experiment 3.

claim: For local questions in Experiment 3, the effect of word-related features and task relevance was more salient for counts of rereading than gaze duration.
source: In contrast, the effect of word-related features and task relevance was more salient for counts of rereading than gaze duration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by analysis of different eye-tracking measures in Experiment 3.

claim: The passage beginning effect was higher for global than local questions in Experiment 3.
source: The passage beginning effect was higher for global than local questions, but the difference was smaller than in Experiment 2 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, p = 2 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for the comparisons across four experiments).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of passage beginning effects in Experiment 3.

claim: The difference in passage beginning effect between global and local questions was smaller in Experiment 3 than in Experiment 2.
source: The passage beginning effect was higher for global than local questions, but the difference was smaller than in Experiment 2 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, p = 2 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for the comparisons across four experiments).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between experiments.

claim: The question relevance effect was smaller for Experiment 3 than Experiment 2.
source: The question relevance effect was also smaller for Experiment 3 than Experiment 2 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, p=2 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for the comparisons across four experiments).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between experiments.

claim: The word reading time of native readers was significantly modulated by the task, but the effect was weaker than that on L2 readers.
source: These results showed that the word reading time of native readers was significantly modulated by the task, but the effect was weaker than that on L2 readers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of results between Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: In Experiment 4, the reading speed was on average 225 ± 40 words/min.
source: The participants were given 1.5 min to preview the passage, and the reading speed was on average 225 ± 40 words/min, lower than that in Experiments 1–3 (p=6 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for comparisons across four experiments).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: The reading speed in Experiment 4 was lower than that in Experiments 1–3.
source: The participants were given 1.5 min to preview the passage, and the reading speed was on average 225 ± 40 words/min, lower than that in Experiments 1–3 (p=6 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for comparisons across four experiments).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of reading speeds across experiments.

claim: During passage preview in Experiment 4, the word reading time was similarly predicted by the pre-trained and fine-tuned transformer-based models.
source: During passage preview, the word reading time was similarly predicted by the pre-trained and fine-tuned transformer-based models (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, the word reading time was significantly predicted by layout and word features, but not question relevance.
source: Furthermore, the word reading time was significantly predicted by layout and word features, but not question relevance (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Supported by regression analysis results in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, both the early and late processing stages of human reading were significantly affected by layout and word features, and the effects were larger for the late processing stage indexed by counts of rereading.
source: Both the early and late processing stages of human reading were significantly affected by layout and word features, and the effects were larger for the late processing stage indexed by counts of rereading (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by analysis of different eye-tracking measures in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, the passage beginning effect was not significantly different between local and global questions.
source: The passage beginning effect was not significantly different between local and global questions (Figure 5C, fourth column, p=0.994, bootstrap, FDR corrected for comparisons across four experiments)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison in Experiment 4.

claim: The question relevance effect in Experiment 4 was significantly smaller than the question relevance effect in Experiments 1–3.
source: and the question relevance effect was significantly smaller than the question relevance effect in Experiments 1–3 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, p=2 × 10–4, bootstrap, FDR corrected for comparisons across four experiments).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison across experiments.

claim: The question relevance effects observed during goal-directed reading were task dependent.
source: These results confirmed that the question relevance effects observed during goal-directed reading were indeed task dependent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison between Experiment 4 and Experiments 1-3.

claim: Human attention distribution can be explained by the attention weights in transformer-based DNN models that are optimized to perform the same reading task but blind to the human eye-tracking data.
source: In this challenging task, it is demonstrated that human attention distribution can be explained by the attention weights in transformer-based DNN models that are optimized to perform the same reading task but blind to the human eye-tracking data.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding, supported by the correlation analyses throughout the manuscript.

claim: When participants scan a passage without knowing the question to answer, their attention distribution can be explained by transformer-based DNN models that are optimized to predict a word based on the context.
source: Furthermore, when participants scan a passage without knowing the question to answer, their attention distribution can also be explained by transformer-based DNN models that are optimized to predict a word based on the context.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 4, supported by the model comparison results.

claim: For humans, basic text features strongly modulate the duration of the first reading of a word.
source: For humans, basic text features strongly modulate the duration of the first reading of a word, while the question relevance of a word only modulates how many times the word is reread, especially for high-proficiency L2 readers compared to native readers.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the analysis of different eye-tracking measures.

claim: The question relevance of a word only modulates how many times the word is reread, especially for high-proficiency L2 readers compared to native readers.
source: For humans, basic text features strongly modulate the duration of the first reading of a word, while the question relevance of a word only modulates how many times the word is reread, especially for high-proficiency L2 readers compared to native readers.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the comparison between Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: Basic text features mainly modulate the attention weights in shallow layers of DNNs.
source: Here, we demonstrate that basic text features mainly modulate the attention weights in shallow layers, while the question relevance of a word modulates the attention weights in deep layers, reflecting hierarchical control of attention to optimize task performance.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the layer-wise analysis of DNN attention.

claim: The question relevance of a word modulates the attention weights in deep layers of DNNs.
source: Here, we demonstrate that basic text features mainly modulate the attention weights in shallow layers, while the question relevance of a word modulates the attention weights in deep layers, reflecting hierarchical control of attention to optimize task performance.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the layer-wise analysis of DNN attention.

claim: The attention weights in both the shallow and deep layers of DNN contribute to the explanation of human word reading time.
source: The attention weights in both the shallow and deep layers of DNN contribute to the explanation of human word reading time (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by the regression analysis showing contributions from multiple layers.

claim: Pre-training leads to text-based attention that can well explain general-purpose reading in Experiment 4.
source: The results show that pre-training leads to text-based attention that can well explain general-purpose reading in Experiment 4, while the fine-tuning process leads to goal-directed attention in Experiments 1–3 (Figures 4B and 5A).
evidence: This is a summary of findings comparing pre-trained and fine-tuned models across experiments.

claim: The fine-tuning process leads to goal-directed attention in Experiments 1–3.
source: The results show that pre-training leads to text-based attention that can well explain general-purpose reading in Experiment 4, while the fine-tuning process leads to goal-directed attention in Experiments 1–3 (Figures 4B and 5A).
evidence: This is a summary of findings comparing pre-trained and fine-tuned models across experiments.

claim: The pre-training task used in all three models analyzed is to predict a word based on the context.
source: Pre-training is also achieved through task optimization, and the pre-training task used in all the three models analyzed here is to predict a word based on the context.
evidence: This is a description of the pre-training procedure for the transformer models, based on established knowledge about these models.

claim: The purpose of the word prediction task is to let models learn the general statistical regularity in a language based on large corpora.
source: The purpose of the word prediction task is to let models learn the general statistical regularity in a language based on large corpora, which is crucial for model performance on downstream tasks (Lan et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019; Devlin et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to the model development literature.

claim: The word prediction pre-training process can naturally introduce the sensitivity to word surprisal.
source: and this process can naturally introduce the sensitivity to word surprisal, that is, how unpredictable a word is given the context.
evidence: This is an inference about how the pre-training task affects model properties.

claim: Previous eye-tracking studies have suggested that the predictability of words can modulate reading time.
source: Previous eye-tracking studies have suggested that the predictability of words, that is, surprisal, can modulate reading time (Hale, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to reading research literature.

claim: Neuroscientific studies have indicated that the cortical responses to language converge with the representations in pre-trained DNN models.
source: and neuroscientific studies have also indicated that the cortical responses to language converge with the representations in pre-trained DNN models (Goldstein et al., 2022; Schrimpf et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to neuroscience literature.

claim: The tokenization process in DNN can contribute to the similarity between human and DNN attention distributions.
source: Additionally, the tokenization process in DNN can also contribute to the similarity between human and DNN attention distributions: DNN first separates words into tokens (e.g., 'tokenization' is separated into 'token' and 'ization').
evidence: This is an explanation of how tokenization affects attention, based on inference about model properties.

claim: Longer words tend to be separated into more tokens in DNNs.
source: Since longer words tend to be separated into more tokens, that is, fragments of frequently co-occurred letters, longer words receive more attention even if the model pay uniform attention to each of its input, that is, a token.
evidence: This is an explanation based on knowledge of how tokenization works in transformer models.

claim: Previous eye-tracking studies have shown that readers fixate longer upon longer words, words of lower-frequency, words that are less predictable based on the context, and words at the beginning of a line.
source: Previous eye-tracking studies have shown that the readers fixate longer upon, for example, longer words, words of lower-frequency, words that are less predictable based on the context, and words at the beginning of a line (Rayner, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to established reading research.

claim: The E-Z reader and SWIFT models have been proposed to predict the eye movements during reading based on basic oculomotor properties or lexical processing.
source: A number of models, for example, the E-Z reader (Reichle et al., 2003) and SWIFT (Engbert et al., 2005), have been proposed to predict the eye movements during reading based on basic oculomotor properties or lexical processing (Reichle et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to eye movement modeling literature.

claim: Some models view reading as an optimization process that minimizes the time or the number of saccades required to read a sentence.
source: Some models also view reading as an optimization process that minimizes the time or the number of saccades required to read a sentence (Legge et al., 2002; Liu and Reichle, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to optimization-based reading models.

claim: A recent study has demonstrated that the specific reading goal modulates the word reading time when readers read a passage to answer a question that can be answered using a word-matching strategy.
source: When readers read a passage to answer a question that can be answered using a word-matching strategy (Hermann et al., 2015), a recent study has demonstrated that the specific reading goal modulates the word reading time and the effect can be modeled using an RNN model (Hahn and Keller, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent reading research.

claim: For challenging questions that cannot be answered using a word-matching strategy, attention is modulated by the reading goal but the attention modulation cannot be explained by a word-matching model.
source: Here, we focus on questions that cannot be answered using a word-matching strategy (Figure 1B) and demonstrate that, for these challenging questions, attention is still modulated by the reading goal but the attention modulation cannot be explained by a word-matching model (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the current study, supported by the model comparison results.

claim: The attention effect for challenging questions is better captured by transformer models than an advanced RNN model (the SAR).
source: Instead, the attention effect is better captured by transformer models than an advanced RNN model, that is, the SAR (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions in the current study.

claim: Previous studies have revealed inconsistent results about whether readers spent more time reading task-relevant sentences when reading a passage with a particular goal or perspective.
source: When human readers read a passage with a particular goal or perspective, previous studies have revealed inconsistent results about whether the readers spent more time reading task-relevant sentences (Yeari et al., 2015; Grabe, 1979; Kaakinen et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous reading research showing mixed findings.

claim: It has been proposed that the question relevance effect weakens for readers with a higher working memory and when readers read a familiar topic.
source: To explain the inconsistent results, it has been proposed that the question relevance effect weakens for readers with a higher working memory and when readers read a familiar topic (Kaakinen et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work explaining variability in reading effects.

claim: Non-native readers spend more time reading question-relevant information than native readers do.
source: Similarly, here, we demonstrate that non-native readers indeed spend more time reading question-relevant information than native readers do (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of results between Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: When readers are more skilled and when the passage is relatively easy to read, their processing is so efficient that they do not need extra time to encode task-relevant information and may rely on covert attention to prioritize the processing of task-relevant information.
source: Therefore, it is possible that when readers are more skilled and when the passage is relatively easy to read, their processing is so efficient so that they do not need extra time to encode task-relevant information and may rely on covert attention to prioritize the processing of task-relevant information.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the differences between native and non-native readers.

claim: Some studies find that the DNN attention weights are positively correlated with the importance of each word.
source: A number of studies have investigated whether the DNN attention weights are interpretable, but the conclusions are mixed: some studies find that the DNN attention weights are positively correlated with the importance of each word (Yang et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to DNN interpretability literature.

claim: Other studies fail to find correlation between DNN attention weights and word importance.
source: while other studies fail to find such correlation (Serrano and Smith, 2019; Jain and Wallace, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to DNN interpretability literature showing negative findings.

claim: Some studies find that the attention weights in the last layer of transformer-based DNN models better correlates with human word reading time than basic word frequency measures.
source: Some studies find that the attention weights in the last layer of transformer-based DNN models better correlates with human word reading time than basic word frequency measures (Bolotova et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to research on DNN attention and human reading.

claim: Integrating human word reading time into DNN can slightly improve task performance.
source: and integrating human word reading time into DNN can slightly improve task performance (Malmaud et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to research on incorporating human data into DNNs.

claim: Other studies find no meaningful correlation between the attention weights in transformer-based DNNs and human word reading time.
source: Other studies, however, find no meaningful correlation between the attention weights in transformer-based DNNs and human word reading time (Sood et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to research showing lack of correlation.

claim: The last layer of transformer-based DNNs is tuned to task relevant information.
source: The current results provide a potential explanation for the discrepancy in the literature: The last layer of transformer-based DNNs is tuned to task relevant information (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by layer-wise analysis of DNN attention in the current study.

claim: The influence of task relevance on word reading time is rather weak for native readers.
source: but the influence of task relevance on word reading time is rather weak for native readers (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of native reader data in Experiment 3.

claim: The correlation between the last-layer DNN attention weights and human reading time may not be robust.
source: Consequently, the correlation between the last-layer DNN attention weights and human reading time may not be robust.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the weak task relevance effect in native readers.

claim: The reading time of both native and non-native readers are reliably modulated by basic text features, which can be modeled by the attention weights in shallower DNN layers.
source: The current results demonstrate that the reading time of both native and non-native readers are reliably modulated by basic text features, which can be modeled by the attention weights in shallower DNN layers.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the layer-wise analysis across experiments.

claim: Transformer-based DNN models can automatically generate human-like attention in the absence of any prior knowledge about the properties of the human reading process.
source: Finally, the current study demonstrates that transformer-based DNN models can automatically generate human-like attention in the absence of any prior knowledge about the properties of the human reading process.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding about task optimization and attention.

claim: Simpler models that fail to explain human performance also fail to predict human attention distribution.
source: Simpler models that fail to explain human performance also fail to predict human attention distribution.
evidence: This is a summary of findings comparing different model types.

claim: Different models can solve the same computational problem using distinct algorithms, and only some algorithms generate human-like attention distribution.
source: It remains possible, however, different models can solve the same computational problem using distinct algorithms, and only some algorithms generate human-like attention distribution.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the relationship between computational solutions and attention.

claim: Sharing similar attention distribution with humans provides a way to interpret the attention weights in computational models.
source: In other words, human-like attention distribution may not be a unique solution to optimize the goal-directed reading task. Sharing similar attention distribution with humans, however, provides a way to interpret the attention weights in computational models.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for model interpretability.

claim: The dataset and methods developed provide an effective probe to test the biological plausibility of NLP models.
source: From this perspective, the dataset and methods developed here provide an effective probe to test the biological plausibility of NLP models that can be easily applied to test whether a model evolves human-like attention distribution.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader implications and applications of the study.

claim: 800 question/passage pairs were adapted from the RACE dataset.
source: In total, 800 question/passage pairs were adapted from the RACE dataset (Lai et al., 2017), a collection of English reading comprehension questions designed for Chinese high school students who learn English as a second language.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials.

claim: The questions fell into six types: three types of local questions and three types of global questions.
source: The questions fell into six types (Figure 1B and C): three types of questions required attention to details, for example, retrieving a fact or generate inference based on a fact, which were referred to as local questions. The other three types of questions concerned the general understanding of a passage, for example, summarizing the main idea or identifying the purpose of writing, which were referred to as global questions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and question categorization.

claim: None of the questions directly appeared in the passage.
source: None of the question directly appeared in the passage, and the longest string that overlapped in the passage and question was 1.8 ± 1.5 words on average.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials showing question difficulty.

claim: Participants in Experiment 1 were Chinese college or graduate students who had relatively high English proficiency.
source: Participants in Experiment 1 were Chinese college or graduate students who had relatively high English proficiency.
evidence: This is a description of the participant population.

claim: Participants selected 'yes' for confidence about answering correctly for 90.47% of questions.
source: Participants selected yes for 90.47% of questions (89.62 and 92.04% for local and global questions, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data on participant confidence ratings.

claim: The mean confidence rating was 3.25 on a scale of 1-4.
source: After answering the question, they also rated their confidence about their answer on the scale of 1–4 (low to high). The mean confidence rating was 3.25 (3.28 and 3.18 for local and global question, respectively), suggesting that the participants were confident about their answers.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on participant confidence ratings.
